title: Interleaved streaming vs batching KV shard walkthrough - Hyperion Networks
summary: Redwood AE+SE and Hyperion infra + platform team ran a deep-dive on p95/p99 spikes tied to KV cache sharding and network hops. We compared streaming vs non-streaming (chunked) modes, examined batching strategies and quantization tradeoffs, and mapped mitigation paths across Dedicated vs VPC private deployments. Agreed next steps: run a focused benchmark (50k request sample) with streaming on vs off, collect KV hit maps, and share a config diff for their autoscaler and batch policy.
topics: VPC on-prem network hop considerations and egress patterns

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Jessa Lin (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Tara Chen (Head of AI - Hyperion), Dev Patel (Infra), Sasha Müller (Platform)

-- Optional auto-summary present (short) --
Summary: quick notes at top: investigating p99 tail spikes, looking at streaming vs batching, KV shard hot spots and network hops; agreed to run benchmark and share artifacts.

-- Transcript body (periodic timestamps) --
[00:00:00] Jessa: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. This is Jessa from Redwood, with Marco our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] Tara: Good, thanks. We're eager to get into the p99 stuff — been noisy in prod.
[00:00:12] Dev: Yeah we've seen intermittent spikes after deploys and when traffic bursts hit a particular prefix.
[00:00:20] Marco: Cool. Quick agenda — characterize the spike, reproduce with a benchmark, look at streaming vs batching, and then KV cache patterns and network hops. If we have time we'll touch quantization.
[00:00:30] Sasha: That's perfect. We also want to understand tradeoffs for Dedicated vs our VPC peered deployment.
[00:00:38] Jessa: Great. Can you describe current infra and how you're calling the API? Lightweight.
[00:00:45] Dev: We're on GCP, VPC peering to Redwood private connectors. Requests come from edge proxies into an API gateway — short payloads, median tokens ~180, but tails up to 700. We use a local micro-cache in front of calls for prompt normalization.
[00:01:02] Tara: We get p95 around 150ms but p99 jumps to 1.2s in bursts, more frequently during afternoon traffic peaks.
[00:01:12] Marco: Sounds like classic tail amplification — small fraction of requests hitting KV misses or cold KV population, and then a multi-hop network path. One question: are you using streaming responses in prod or the full non-streaming generation?
[00:01:26] Dev: We're currently non-streaming, wait-for-full. We tried streaming in alpha but have some client-side buffering that made it messy.
[00:01:35] Marco: Okay, that matters. Streaming often reduces perceived latency and can keep backend work pipelined, but it changes batching behavior in the runtime.
[00:01:45] [00:02:15] Speaker 1: Can we get a quick sketch of the call path?
[00:02:20] Sasha: Sure — client -> edge -> gateway -> VPC peer -> Redwood private ingress -> serving cluster -> maybe a KV cache lookup -> runtime -> return. On a KV miss we also hit a long-tail storage call to our index store.
[00:02:38] Marco: That 2nd hop to object storage or index store is the usual culprit. If the KV cache is sharded unevenly, a hotshard can serially slow many in-flight requests.
[00:02:47] Jessa: Can you share your current KV shard distribution? Even rough numbers?
[00:02:52] Dev: Rough — 64 shards, but top 5 shards get ~46% of hits during our recommendation flows.
[00:03:00] Marco: That explains it. Batching helps to amortize kernel overhead but exacerbates head-of-line blocking if a hot shard introduces extra latency into a batch.
[00:03:10] Tara: So streaming might help because smaller partial tokens flow back faster? But then you lose some batching efficiency?
[00:03:18] Marco: Exactly — streaming pipelines token generation and can hide KV miss cost from the perceived latency, but overall throughput cost per token can increase slightly if batching drops. We usually see p95 improve but p99 depends on whether the slow events are clustered.
[00:03:30] [00:04:00] Speaker 2: Is quantization in play?
[00:04:03] Marco: We have a quantized int8 path. It reduces GPU compute time — useful for throughput — but it sometimes changes kernel selection and increases variance on large sequences. For tails that are KV-miss + long sequences, quantization may reduce average latency but not p99 in some cases.
[00:04:20] Dev: We're running a mixed model setup — quantized smaller models for lower tiers, FP16 for the larger ones.
[00:04:27] Marco: That mix makes diagnosis trickier. Also worth checking KV cache key entropy: if keys include session timestamps or ephemeral context, the cache will be less effective.
[00:04:36] [00:05:00] Jessa: We're going to propose a benchmark: 50k mixed requests with the same token distribution you see in prod, run with streaming on and off, and capture per-request timelines plus KV hit maps. We'll also test with batching at 8, 16, 32.
[00:05:13] Tara: Sounds good. How do you instrument KV hit map?
[00:05:16] Marco: We'll add lightweight tracing to log shard id and hit/miss events (low overhead): attach counts per shard and per-minute histograms. We can provide a small script to visualize hot spots.
[00:05:27] Dev: If you can include network hop breakdown (client->ingress->serve->kv->storage) that would be amazing. Some of our logs don't correlate request ids end-to-end.
[00:05:36] Marco: We'll instrument request IDs and show an example waterfall. Expect about 5–7% extra overhead for tracing.
[00:05:44] [00:06:15] Sasha: On networking — we've noticed p99 only on peered VPC traffic, not on public hosted calls. Is that weird?
[00:06:22] Marco: Not too weird. VPC peering constrains routing; you can get asymmetric routing and extra NAT hops depending on how peering is configured. Also MTU differences can cause fragmentation and jitter.
[00:06:33] Jessa: We'll look at hop counts and suggest a minimal change set for peering (route preferences, avoid hairpinning). Also confirm whether you have cross-region endpoints.
[00:06:42] Dev: We're single region for now, but we've got a fail-over region in EU.
[00:06:46] [00:07:15] Speaker 3: Let's talk mitigation strategies — short term and long term.
[00:07:20] Marco: Short term: 1) Enable streaming for latency-sensitive routes where clients can handle partial tokens; 2) Reduce batch size for those routes to avoid head-of-line blocking; 3) Implement dynamic shard rebalancer or add a lightweight in-memory LRU to absorb spikes.
[00:07:36] Tara: Dynamic rebalancer — that sounds heavy. How disruptive is that?
[00:07:40] Marco: Our suggestion is not a full re-shard in prod but a temporary hot-shard redirect — route requests for the top hot keys to a warmed partition or cache layer. It can be transparent and low-risk.
[00:07:52] Dev: Can Redwood route by policy? For example route by token length or by customer tier?
[00:07:57] Jessa: Yes, we have smart routing — latency-first or cost-first policies, and you can pin routes. For your case we can create a latency-first policy for that recommendation endpoint and fallback to a smaller model on overload.
[00:08:08] [00:08:40] Marco: Another long-term: tune kernel selection and quantization profiles per sequence-length distribution. If you have many mid-length sequences, certain kernels perform better. Our runtime can auto-select kernel families, but your workload triggers suboptimal ones in rare paths.
[00:08:55] Sasha: How often does the runtime re-evaluate kernel selection?
[00:08:59] Marco: Per model start and optionally per sequence-length bucket if configured. We can force a trigger as part of a canary if you want.
[00:09:08] [00:09:45] Dev: Any guidance on batching policy thresholds?
[00:09:49] Marco: For perceived latency, batch size around 8 is a sweet spot for your median token lengths; for max throughput use 32 or 64 with preemption windows. Also enable adaptive batching so short requests don't wait too long for the batch to fill.
[00:10:01] Jessa: We'll include a recommended batch config in the runbook.
[00:10:05] [00:10:30] Speaker 4: Can we look at an example timeline of a p99 event?
[00:10:35] Marco: Sure — here's an illustrative timeline: 0ms client->ingress, 12ms ingress->serve routing, 30ms KV lookup returns (if hit), 120ms model kernel execution for tokens 1-200, ~200–400ms for long sequences, but on a KV miss you add 150–400ms for storage fetch depending on coldness, plus network hop jitter. If multiple requests pile on the same hot shard, queuing adds 50–200ms per request.
[00:11:00] Dev: That queuing is exactly what we've seen, and it seems correlated with certain user cohorts.
[00:11:06] Marco: Cohort-based hot keys are common — personalization keys or trending items. We should consider probabilistic pre-warming of those keys.
[00:11:13] [00:12:00] Jessa: Quick question from Sales: are there any compliance blockers for you on using Redwood Private?
[00:12:06] Tara: We need SOC2 type II, SSO via SAML, and KMS integration for key management. Also audit logs retention for 18 months.
[00:12:15] Jessa: We have all of those. We'll attach our compliance pack.
[00:12:20] Dev: For VPC peering, we might need a network security review; we'll loop in security after the benchmark.
[00:12:26] [00:13:00] Marco: Back to streaming vs batching — one nuance: streaming increases concurrency because partial token frames are sent earlier. That helps p95 but increases open connections and kernel context switching. For GPU-bound workloads with many small requests streaming can improve the user experience but increase GPU utilization.
[00:13:18] Sasha: So we may pay more for better p95?
[00:13:21] Marco: Exactly — it's a cost-latency trade. We'll quantify it in the bench.
[00:13:30] [00:14:00] Speaker 5: Any pitfalls with quantization and accuracy regressions?
[00:14:03] Marco: We typically recommend running a small eval set when flipping quantization profiles. Some workloads are sensitive to the 8-bit transform, especially generation with many long-context tokens. We'll include a short eval in the runbook.
[00:14:16] Tara: For our product, occasional output variance is tolerable, but we need to monitor quality regressions over time.
[00:14:22] Jessa: Redwood Optimize can run continual quality checks and send regression alerts tied to your prompt set. We'll include that option in pricing.
[00:14:30] [00:15:00] Marco: Another observation: KV miss penalties can be softened by prefix caching of the most common prompt headers. If you can normalize prompt prefixes server-side, the effective cache hit rate improves.
[00:15:10] Dev: We do some normalization but not full; we'll add it to the bench mod.
[00:15:20] [00:16:00] Jessa: Logistics — we'll share a small script to generate the 50k request workload, plus the KV instrumentation hooks. The bench will run in your environment hitting Redwood private endpoints. We'll provide expected results and a dashboard.
[00:16:14] Tara: Regarding Dedicated vs Private -- if we go with Dedicated reserved capacity, will that change routing topology?
[00:16:22] Marco: Dedicated yields predictable capacity in our pools and reduces noisy neighbor effects. For VPC peered Private you still have network path variability. Dedicated doesn't remove network hops if you're peered, but you get capacity isolation which reduces queueing on the serving side.
[00:16:38] [00:17:00] Dev: Any quick wins we can do before the bench?
[00:17:03] Marco: Yes: temporarily lower batch sizes for the recommendation endpoint, enable early streaming for that route, and add a small LRU in front of KV for the top 5% keys. Those are low risk and reversible.
[00:17:14] Sasha: We'll try lowering batch size today and report back.
[00:17:20] [00:18:00] Speaker 6: Discussion about tracing IDs and correlation.
[00:18:05] Marco: We'll standardize on a request-id header that flows through SDK and our runtime. We'll give you a guide to key your logs to that id.
[00:18:12] Dev: That will help.
[00:18:20] [00:20:00] Jessa: Wrapping up — recap next steps and owners. Marco will deliver the autoscaler diff, I will send the bench and runbook, Dev will run bench and KV map, Tara will confirm security stakeholders. We'll reconvene with results.
[00:20:18] Tara: Sounds good. Thanks.
[00:20:22] Jessa: One last note — we'll attach a sample waterfall and an example of streaming-on vs streaming-off traces so you can see the perceived latency difference.
[00:20:29] Dev: Appreciate it.
[00:20:33] [00:21:00] -- End of main discussion --
[00:21:00] (recording continues, then short Q&A)
[00:22:15] Speaker 7: Quick Q: If we discover a KV hot key, is live re-shard safe?
[00:22:20] Marco: Live full re-shard is heavy. We prefer hot-shard redirect or warming a shadow cache and then cutover during low traffic window.
[00:22:28] Dev: We'll plan for warm redirects.
[00:22:33] [00:30:00] (distributed bench plan sequencing and scheduling, low-volume talk)
[00:35:00] Marco: We'll also include guidance on kernel selection—if you want we can run an A/B on quant profiles to measure p95/p99 delta.
[00:35:10] Tara: Please do.
[00:35:20] [00:45:00] (discussion continues, small clarifications, mention of SOC2 docs)
[00:50:00] Jessa: I'll upload compliance pack and bench links to the shared notes. Link: https://redwood.ai/bench/hpn-9984 (demo link placeholder)
[00:55:00] Sasha: We'll review and pick a date for the run.
[01:00:00] Dev: Any other blockers?
[01:00:06] Tara: Not from our side. Security will need to confirm VPC peering config.
[01:00:15] Jessa: Great. Thanks everyone.
